## Intro
A <i>polygon</i> is a closed planar figure with a boundary of straight segments.
Most polygons we have encountered are triangles, and a few <i>quadrilaterals</i> (4 sided figures).
The segments that form the boundary are <i>sides</i>.
These meet at <i>vertices</i> to form <i>interior angles</i> that are 'inside' the polygon.
To each interior angle under $180^\circ$ are 2  <i>exterior angles</i>, formed by extending either side.
A <i>convex</i> polygon has all its interior angles measure under $180^\circ$. They are our main focus.
Polygons that are not convex are <i>concave</i>.
A <i>diagonal</i> is any segment that joins 2 non adjacent sides.
In a <i>regular</i> polygon, all sides have equal length and all angles equal measure.
As we have seen, a regular polygon with 3 sides is an equilateral triangle, and a regular quadrilateral is a square.
Below, ABDC is a convex polygon (quadrilateral), ABEC is a concave polygon, $\angle ABD$ is an interior angle of ABDC, and $\angle ABF$ is 1 corresponding exterior angle.
$\overline{BC}$ is a diagonal.

```{python}
#| echo: false
img=np.ones((400,400,3),dtype=np.uint8)*255
a=np.array((220,50))
b=(100,290)
c=(340,290)
d=(220,350)
e=(220,230)
f=(60,270)
draw_path(img,f,d,c,a,b,e,c)
cv2.line(img,b,c,color)
for j,lbl in enumerate('ABECFD'):
    p=globals()[lbl.lower()]
    q=20 if j%2 else -10
    cv2.putText(img,lbl,(p[0],p[1]+q),font,0.6,color,2)
cv2.circle(img,f,radius=4,color=color,thickness=-1)
show_geometry_image(img)
```

## Polygon angles

::: {#lem-9.ngon.angle}

For any n-gon, the sum of its interior angles is $180(n-2)^\circ$, and the sum of its exterior angles is $360^\circ$.
In particular, in a regular n-gon, each interior angle is $180(n-2)^\circ/n$, and each exterior angle is $360^\circ /n$.

:::

This result suggests that sometimes it is easier to consider a polygon's exterior than interior angles.

::: {.proof}

Any n-gon can be split into n-2 triangles (for a convex polygon, the segments that do this splitting are the diagonals from a fixed vertex).
Since the sum of a triangle's angles is $180^\circ$ by @lem-2.5, it is $180(n-2)^\circ$ for an n-gon.
Since an interior angle and its exterior angle form a straight angle, the sum of an n-gon's exterior angles is (in degrees) $180n-180(n-2)=360$.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
img=np.ones((400,400,3),dtype=np.uint8)*255
a=(200,60)
b=(80,120)
c=(80,320)
d=(320,320)
e=(320,120)
f=(60,270)
cv2.line(img,a,(360,140),color,thickness=2)
cv2.line(img,b,(240,40),color,thickness=2)
cv2.line(img,c,(80,80),color,thickness=2)
cv2.line(img,d,(40,320),color,thickness=2)
cv2.line(img,e,(320,360),color,thickness=2)
draw_path(img,e,b,d,thickness=1)
show_geometry_image(img)
```

## Polygon area

::: {#lem-9.ngon.ctr}

A regular n-gon has a center that is equidistant from each vertex, equidistant from each side, and the angle bisector at each vertex passes thru this center.
If n is even, then this angle bisector is also the angle bisector for the opposite vertex (n/2 vertices away).<br>
An n-gon is regular if and only if it can be split into n congruent isosceles triangles, with each side as a base.

:::

Any regular polygon thus has a unique circle that circumscribes it, and another unique circle that can be inscribed in it.
The inradius is often called the <i>apothem</i>. Below, $\overline{GO}$ is an apothem.

::: {.proof}

Let A B C be consecutive vertices on the polygon. Draw angle bisectors for $\angle A$ and $\angle B$ (which have the same measure), call their intersection O.
Draw $\overline{OC}$. Since AB=BC, we have $\triangle ABO \cong \triangle BCO$ by ASA congruence @lem-3.asa.
Then AO=BO=CO and $m \angle BCO=m \angle ABO$ by @lem-3.6.isosc and CPCTC, so $\overline{CO}$ bisects $\angle C$.
If we connect O to each of the polygon's vertices via segments, we get n congruent isosceles triangles, each with vertex angle $360^\circ /n$.
When n is even, n/2 of these add up to $180^\circ$, so $\overline{AO}$ and the segment to the opposite vertex form a straight angle.
The distance from O to any of the polygon's sides is the 'height' of any of these isosceles triangles with that side as the 'base'.
This distance (or the triangle's altitude) is precisely the apothem.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
img=np.ones((400,400,3),dtype=np.uint8)*255
o=(200,200)
hx=reg_poly(6,o,150)
e,f,a,b,c,d=hx
g=(200,60) #midpt(c,d)
draw_path(img,*hx,e)
draw_path(img,a,o,b,thickness=1)
draw_path(img,c,o,(200,70),thickness=1)
add_tick(img,a,o)
add_tick(img,b,o)
cv2.ellipse(img,a,(25,25),0,240,360,color,thickness=1) #angle markers
cv2.ellipse(img,b,(25,25),0,-60,60,color,thickness=1)
draw_path(img,(200,90),(180,90),(180,70),thickness=1) #perp marker
for j,lbl in enumerate('AGBOC'):
    p1=globals()[lbl.lower()]
    q=10 if j%2 else -20
    cv2.putText(img,lbl,(p1[0]+q,p1[1]),font,0.6,color,2)
show_geometry_image(img)
```

::: {#lem-9.apothem}

A regular polygon area is its apothem times its semi perimeter.

:::

::: {.proof}

Continuing from @lem-9.ngon.ctr where we split the polygon into n congruent isosceles triangles, its area is $n[APO]=n \cdot AB \cdot GO/2$ by @lem-4.tri.area.
We recognize $n \cdot AB/2$ as the semi perimeter and GO as the apothem.

:::

Just as with Heron's formula, @lem-9.apothem might not be the best way to find a polygon's area.

::: {#exm-9.3.hexagon}

A regular hexagon's 3 'long' diagonals (that connect opposite vertices) split it into 6 congruent equilateral triangles.<br>
Problem solving with regular hexagons often uses this.
Find its area in terms of its side length s.
If A B C D are consecutive vertices, find AD and AC.

:::


::: {.proof}

Draw 6 segments to connect the hexagon's center to its 6 vertices.
These produce the 3 long diagonals, which split the hexagon into 6 isosceles triangles by @lem-9.ngon.ctr.
Each of the hexagon's angles is $120^\circ$ by @lem-9.ngon.angle. So each isosceles triangle's base angles are $60^\circ$, so they are in fact equilateral.

:::

::: {#exm-9.3.octagon}

Use the below diagram (prove the outer figure is a square) to find a regular octagon's area in terms of its side length s.
Find the length of its apothem and any segment from its center to a vertex.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
img=np.ones((400,400,3),dtype=np.uint8)*255
oc=reg_poly(8,(200,200),150,22.5)
a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h=oc
draw_path(img,*oc,a)
draw_path(img,a,(339,339),b,thickness=1)
draw_path(img,c,(61,339),d,thickness=1)
draw_path(img,e,(61,61),f,thickness=1)
draw_path(img,g,(339,61),h,thickness=1)
show_geometry_image(img)
```
2 more strategies to find area are to break the figure into more manageable pieces (usually triangles and quadrilaterals), or to consider a larger figure and view the desired figure as a 'leftover' portion.
Regular polygons have many symmetries useful for problem solving.

::: {#exr-9.3.5}

A <i>hexagram</i> is formed with 2 congruent equilateral triangles that trisect each other's sides.
Prove the intersection is a regular hexagon. Find the ratio of the hexagram's area to the hexagon's.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false

a,b,c,d,e,f=hx
draw_path(img,a,c,e,a)
draw_path(img,b,d,f,b)

```

Aside: any 2 polygons with the same area can be dissected into the same pieces.
The case where 1 is an equilateral triangle and the other is a square is the "haberdasher's problem" and shown below.
See more <a href=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Dissection.html>here</a>.

## Polygon construction

::: {#exm-9.5.square}

To construct a square, we know how to make 4 segments of the same length that are perpendicular @exm-6.6.perp.<br>
A slicker way is to draw 2 perpendicular lines, and then a circle centered at their intersection.
Connect the 4 points where the circle intersects the lines.

:::

::: {.proof}

This makes 4 congruent 45-45-90 triangles @lem-6.45tri, so we have 4 sides of the same length that are perpendicular, ie a square.

::: 

```{python}
#| echo: false
img=np.ones((400,400,3),dtype=np.uint8)*255
a=(340,200)
cv2.line(img,(200,30),(200,370),color)
cv2.line(img,(30,200),(370,200),color)
cv2.circle(img,(200,200),radius=140,color=color)
img1=img.copy()
draw_path(img,a,(200,340),(60,200),(200,60),a)
draw_path(img,(200,180),(220,180),(220,200), thickness=1) #perp marker
show_geometry_image(img)
```

::: {#exm-9.5.hexagon}

To construct a regular hexagon, due to @exm-9.3.hexagon, we can construct 6 equilateral triangles with a vertex shared by all 6 using @lem-3.7.
A slicker way is to draw $\odot O$, pick any point A on it. Find the other 2 points on $\odot O$ that are OA away from A.
Keep going until we have 6 points on $\odot O$ all spaced OA apart. Finally, connect these 6 points.
So for the whole construction, have the compass opened to the same radius.

:::

::: {.proof}

By construction, if we connect each vertex to O, we get 6 equilateral triangles.
So we have a regular hexagon by @exm-9.3.hexagon.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
img=np.ones((400,400,3),dtype=np.uint8)*255
o=(200,200)
hx=reg_poly(6,o,150)
draw_path(img,*hx,hx[0])
cv2.circle(img,(200,200),radius=150,color=color)
cv2.ellipse(img,hx[0],(150,150),0,210,270,color)
for j in range(4):
    cv2.ellipse(img,hx[j],(150,150),0,90+60*j,150+60*j,color)
cv2.circle(img,o,radius=4,color=color,thickness=-1)
cv2.putText(img,'O',(210,200),font,0.6,color,2)
cv2.putText(img,'A',(330,200),font,0.6,color,2)
show_geometry_image(img)
```

::: {#exm-9.5.octagon}

To construct a regular octagon, we can draw 8 segments of equal length and with $135^\circ$ angles.
We can make these by doing $90^\circ$ angles 1st, and then bisecting the exterior angles @exm-7.7.abisect.
A slicker way is to start with the perpendicular lines and circle as we did to construct a square @exm-9.5.square.
Then draw angle bisectors (2 lines) for the 4 right angles.
Connecting the 8 points of intersection with the circle gives a regular octagon.

:::

::: {.proof}

By construction, if we connect each vertex to the circle's center (where the 4 lines intersect), we get 8 congruent isosceles triangles.
They form a regular octagon by @lem-9.ngon.ctr.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
cv2.line(img1,(30,30),(370,370),color)
cv2.line(img1,(30,370),(370,30),color)
oc=reg_poly(8,(200,200),140)
draw_path(img1,*oc,oc[0])
show_geometry_image(img1)
```

## More problems

::: {#exr-9.6}

A square and regular hexagon have the same side length. The square's area is $\sqrt{3}$. What is the hexagon's?<br>

If a regular octagon has consecutive vertices A B C D E, and AB=1, find AC AD AE.<br>
A regular polygon has the same number of diagonals as sides. What is the sum of its interior angle measures?<br>

They share side $\overline{AB}$. What are the possible values of $m \angle CBD$?
What about if pentagon -> square, hexagon -> pentagon?<br>
Given regular octagon ABCDEFGH, if $\overline{AE}$ and $\overline{CG}$ intersect at O and M is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$, find $m \angle BAO$, $m \angle AOM$, $m \angle MOD$.
(Hint: prove O is the center of ABCDEFGH)

Aside: a <i>tessellation/ tiling</i> covers a surface (usually a plane) with shapes called <i>tiles</i> with neither gaps nor overlaps.
A <i>regular tessellation</i> uses just 1 regular polygon as a tile, eg a hexagon as in @exr-9.7.46 (the only other possibilities are squares or equilateral triangles).
A <i>semiregular tessellation</i> can use 1+ kinds of regular polygons, with the same order of them surrounding each vertex.
Not counting regular tessellations, there are 8 possibilities, eg with squares and octagons as below.
A <i>demiregular tessellation</i> can use 1+ kinds of regular polygons, but allows different kinds to surround each vertex.
An example can be made by repeating the pattern in @exr-9.7.40.
But tilings need not use only use regular polygons, or be <i>periodic</i> (ie, repeat the same pattern over and over).
See the 'tessellation' Wikipedia page for more examples, or <a href=https://www.mcescher.com>this</a>.

```{python}
#| echo: false
img=np.ones((500,500,3),dtype=np.uint8)*255
oc=reg_poly(8,(110,110),100,22.5)
dx=np.array([184,0])
dy=dx[::-1]
oc2=oc+dx
for q in [oc,oc2,oc+dy,oc2+dy]:
```
